questions.q: State what is meant by defensive design.

markPoints.concept: writing a program so that it copes with being used wrongly
markPoints.exemplar: Writing a program so that it anticipates being used wrongly.

questions.example: Writing a program so that it anticipates the mistakes and misuse it will meet, and copes with them rather than crashing.
questions.paraphrase: Designing code that expects users to do unexpected things and handles it.
questions.feedback: Anticipating misuse. A program that only works when everything goes right has not been designed defensively.
questions.revisitLabel: 2.3 Lesson 2 — Cyber defence HQ, station 1: Anticipating misuse

questions.q: Which of these are part of designing a program defensively? Tick all that apply.
options: Validating every input before using it
Checking that a file exists before opening it
Giving a helpful message when something goes wrong
Requiring users to authenticate before reaching private data
Writing the program in as few lines as possible
Making the program run as fast as possible
correct: Validating every input before using it
Checking that a file exists before opening it
Giving a helpful message when something goes wrong
Requiring users to authenticate before reaching private data
questions.feedback: Speed and brevity are not defences. A short fast program that crashes on bad input is not robust.
questions.revisitLabel: 2.3 Lesson 2 — Cyber defence HQ, station 1: Anticipating misuse

questions.q: Explain why a program should check that a file exists before trying to open it.

markPoints.concept: opening a file that is not there causes an error
markPoints.exemplar: Trying to open a file that is not there causes an error.

markPoints.concept: so the program can give a sensible message instead of stopping
markPoints.exemplar: Checking first means that the program can tell the user instead of crashing.

questions.example: If the file is missing, trying to open it raises an error and the program stops. Checking first lets it tell the user that the file could not be found and carry on, which is far better than crashing in front of them.
questions.paraphrase: Attempting to open a non-existent file throws an error that halts the program, so testing for it first allows a sensible message to be shown and execution to continue.
questions.feedback: What goes wrong, and what checking lets you do instead.
questions.revisitLabel: 2.3 Lesson 2 — Cyber defence HQ, station 1: Anticipating misuse

questions.q: A website asks a user to type a word shown in a distorted image. What is this for?
options: To check that the user is a person rather than an automated program
To check that the user's keyboard works
To encrypt the user's password before sending it
To validate the format of the user's email address
questions.feedback: A CAPTCHA defends against bots submitting the form thousands of times.
questions.revisitLabel: 2.3 Lesson 2 — Cyber defence HQ, station 1: Anticipating misuse

questions.q: Which of these are ways a program can authenticate a user? Tick all that apply.
options: A username and password
A code sent to the user's phone
A fingerprint or face scan
Answering a security question set earlier
Checking that the username is spelled correctly
Checking that the password is at least eight characters long
correct: A code sent to the user's phone
Answering a security question set earlier
questions.feedback: Authentication proves who somebody is. The last two are validation: they check the entry makes sense, not who typed it.
questions.revisitLabel: 2.3 Lesson 2 — Cyber defence HQ, station 3: Authentication

questions.q: Explain why a program should store a hashed version of a password rather than the password itself.

markPoints.concept: if the stored data is read the actual passwords are not in it
accept: not the password|passwords are not|no passwords|not in it|not stored|cannot see|cannot read|does not have|hash|hashes|hashed|scrambled|unreadable
markPoints.exemplar: If the stored data is stolen, the actual passwords are not in it.

markPoints.concept: because a hash cannot practically be turned back into the original
accept: cannot be reversed|not be reversed|cannot be turned back|not be turned back|cannot turn it back|cannot be worked backwards|not be worked backwards|cannot be undone|one way|oneway|cannot get back|cannot work out|cannot undo|impossible to|very hard to
markPoints.exemplar: This is because a hash cannot practically be turned back into the password.

questions.example: If the file of accounts is stolen, what the attacker has is a list of hashes, and a hash cannot practically be turned back into the password it came from. The program can still check a login, because it hashes what was typed and compares the two hashes rather than the passwords.
questions.paraphrase: Should the stored records be taken, they contain no usable passwords, since the process of producing a hash cannot be worked backwards.
questions.feedback: What a thief gets, and why it is no use to them.
questions.revisitLabel: 2.3 Lesson 2 — Cyber defence HQ, station 3: Authentication

questions.q: Which of these can go wrong while a program is running, however carefully it was written? Tick all that apply.
options: The user enters something unexpected
A file the program needs has been moved or deleted
The network connection drops part-way through
A calculation ends up dividing by zero
The program's syntax is wrong
The programmer has not finished writing it
correct: A file the program needs has been moved or deleted
The network connection drops part-way through
A calculation ends up dividing by zero
questions.feedback: These are run-time problems: they depend on what happens while the program runs. A syntax error stops it running at all.
questions.subtopic: When things go wrong at run time
questions.revisitReason: When things go wrong at run time
questions.revisitLabel: 2.3 Lesson 2 — Cyber defence HQ, station 2: When things go wrong

questions.q: A program asks the user for two numbers and divides the first by the second. What should it check before dividing?
options: That the second number is not zero
That the first number is larger than the second
That both numbers are whole numbers
That the user has entered them in order
questions.feedback: Dividing by zero stops the program. Checking for it first is defensive design in one line.
